formulas.name: Arithmetic mean

variables.name: sum of the values
variables.description: Σx, all the data values added together.

variables.name: number of values
variables.description: How many data values there are.

formulas.explanation: The mean shares the total equally among all the values: add them up and divide by how many there are. It is the balance point of the data on a number line. A single extreme value can pull it a long way, which is why the median is sometimes preferred.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to summarise a typical value of numerical data without strong outliers.

example.story: Five students scored a total of 340 points on a quiz. What is the mean score?

formulas.name: Weighted mean of two values

variables.name: weighted mean
variables.description: The average with each value counted according to its weight.

formulas.explanation: In a weighted mean some values count more than others. Multiply each value by its weight, add, and divide by the total weight. With equal weights it is the ordinary mean; the same pattern extends to any number of values.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for course grades with weighted components, averages of grouped data, or combining means of groups of different sizes.

example.story: An exam counts 60 % and coursework 40 %. A student scores 80 on the exam and 70 on the coursework. What is the final grade?
steps: Total weight is 1, so the grade is 76

formulas.name: Population variance

variables.name: population standard deviation
variables.description: σ is the standard deviation; σ² is the variance.

variables.name: sum of squared deviations
variables.description: Σ(x - μ)², the squared distances from the mean added up.

variables.name: population size
variables.description: Number of values in the whole population.

formulas.explanation: Variance measures spread: it is the average squared distance of the values from their mean. Squaring stops positive and negative deviations from cancelling and makes big deviations count more. Its square root, the standard deviation σ, is back in the units of the data.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it when your data is the entire population, not a sample from a larger group.
assumptions: data is the whole population (for a sample divide by n - 1)

example.story: The values 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 have mean 5 and squared deviations adding up to 32. Find the variance and standard deviation.

formulas.name: Sample variance

variables.name: sample standard deviation
variables.description: s is the standard deviation; s² is the variance.

variables.name: sum of squared deviations
variables.description: Σ(x - x̄)², using the sample mean.

variables.name: sample size
variables.description: Number of values in the sample (at least 2).

formulas.explanation: When the data is a sample, deviations are measured from the sample mean, which sits a little closer to the data than the true mean does. Dividing by n - 1 instead of n (Bessel's correction) compensates, so s² is an unbiased estimate of the population variance.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it whenever your data is a sample used to estimate the spread of a larger population, which is the usual case.

example.story: A sample has values 2, 4, 6, 8 (mean 5, squared deviations totalling 20). Estimate the population standard deviation.

formulas.name: Population standard deviation (computational form)

variables.name: sum of squares
variables.description: Σx², each value squared and then added.

formulas.explanation: Expanding Σ(x - μ)² shows that the variance equals the mean of the squares minus the square of the mean. This form is quicker by hand because you only need Σx and Σx², which calculators keep as you enter data. Take the square root for the standard deviation.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it with summary statistics (Σx, Σx², n), for example from a calculator's statistics mode or a frequency table.
assumptions: watch for rounding errors when the mean is large compared with the spread

example.story: For the values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5: Σx² = 55, n = 5 and μ = 3. Find σ.

tags: mean of squares minus square of mean

formulas.name: Sample standard deviation (computational form)

variables.name: sum of squares
variables.description: Σx², each value squared and then added.

formulas.explanation: The sum of squared deviations Σ(x - x̄)² equals Σx² - n x̄². Dividing by n - 1 and taking the square root gives the sample standard deviation from summary statistics. Calculators label it s or σₙ₋₁.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to estimate a population's spread from sample totals, for example in experiments and surveys.

example.story: A sample 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 has Σx² = 55, n = 5 and x̄ = 3. Find s.

formulas.name: Coefficient of variation

variables.name: coefficient of variation
variables.description: Spread relative to the size of the mean.

formulas.explanation: The coefficient of variation expresses the standard deviation as a percentage of the mean. Because it has no units, it lets you compare the variability of quantities measured on different scales, such as the weights of mice and of elephants.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to compare the consistency of measurements with very different means or units.
assumptions: data on a ratio scale with a positive mean

example.story: Bags of flour have mean mass 50 (in tenths of a kg) and standard deviation 4. What is the coefficient of variation?

formulas.name: Upper fence for outliers (1.5 IQR rule)

variables.name: upper fence
variables.description: Values above this are flagged as outliers.

variables.name: upper quartile
variables.description: The value three quarters of the way through the sorted data.

variables.name: lower quartile
variables.description: The value one quarter of the way through the sorted data.

formulas.explanation: The interquartile range Q₃ - Q₁ measures the spread of the middle half of the data. Values more than 1.5 IQRs above the upper quartile are unusually large and are commonly treated as outliers. The lower fence is Q₁ - 1.5 IQR. Box plots draw their whiskers up to these limits.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to identify outliers before choosing summary statistics or drawing a box plot.
assumptions: a convention (Tukey's rule), not a law

example.story: Commute times have Q₁ = 20 min and Q₃ = 32 min. Above what time is a commute an outlier?

formulas.name: Z-score (standard score)

variables.name: z-score
variables.description: How many standard deviations x is above (or below) the mean.

formulas.explanation: A z-score measures position relative to the mean in units of standard deviations. Subtracting the mean shifts the centre to zero and dividing by σ rescales the spread to 1. For a normal distribution, this standardisation lets one table of probabilities serve every mean and standard deviation.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to compare results from different tests, to look up normal probabilities, or to spot unusual values (|z| > 2 or 3).

example.story: A test has mean 70 and standard deviation 8. How many standard deviations above the mean is a score of 82?

formulas.name: Normal distribution density

variables.name: probability density
variables.description: Height of the bell curve at x (not itself a probability).

formulas.explanation: The normal (Gaussian) distribution is the familiar bell curve, symmetric about μ with width set by σ. The factor in front makes the total area under the curve equal to 1. Probabilities are areas under the curve, not heights; about 68 % of values lie within one σ of the mean and 95 % within two.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to plot the bell curve, compare likelihoods of values, or model measurement errors and many natural quantities.
assumptions: the data is approximately normally distributed

example.story: What is the height of the standard normal curve (μ = 0, σ = 1) at x = 1?

formulas.name: Standardising a sample mean

variables.name: test statistic
variables.description: Standard score of the sample mean.

variables.name: sample size
variables.description: Number of values in the sample.

formulas.explanation: Means of samples vary less than single values: their standard deviation is σ/√n, the standard error. Standardising a sample mean with that smaller spread tells you how surprising the sample is if the population mean really is μ. By the central limit theorem this works for large samples even when the data is not normal.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for hypothesis tests about a mean when the population standard deviation is known (a z-test).
assumptions: normal population or large n (central limit theorem)

example.story: A machine fills bags with mean 500 g and σ = 20 g. A sample of 16 bags has mean 508 g. What is the z value?

formulas.name: One-sample t statistic

variables.name: t statistic
variables.description: Standardised distance of the sample mean from μ.

variables.name: hypothesised mean
variables.description: The population mean under the null hypothesis.

variables.name: sample standard deviation
variables.description: Standard deviation computed from the sample.

formulas.explanation: When σ is unknown it is estimated by the sample standard deviation s. The extra uncertainty means the statistic follows Student's t distribution with n - 1 degrees of freedom, which has heavier tails than the normal distribution. For large samples t and z become almost the same.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to test a claim about a mean, or to compare a measured mean with a reference value, when the population spread is unknown.

example.story: 16 measurements have mean 10.4 and s = 1.2. Test against a claimed mean of 10: what is t?
steps: Compare with the t distribution with 15 degrees of freedom

formulas.name: Standard error of the mean

variables.name: standard error
variables.description: Standard deviation of the sample mean.

variables.name: standard deviation
variables.description: Spread of individual values (use s if σ is unknown).

formulas.explanation: Averaging n independent values cancels out some of their random variation. The spread of the mean shrinks with the square root of n, so four times as many measurements halve the uncertainty. This is why repeating measurements improves precision, but with diminishing returns.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to give the uncertainty of an average, and inside confidence intervals and hypothesis tests.

example.story: Individual measurements have a standard deviation of 12. What is the standard error of the mean of 36 measurements?

formulas.name: Margin of error for a mean

variables.name: margin of error
variables.description: Half the width of the confidence interval.

variables.name: critical value
variables.description: From the normal distribution: 1.645 for 90 %, 1.96 for 95 %, 2.576 for 99 % confidence.

variables.name: sample size
variables.description: Number of values in the sample.

formulas.explanation: The margin of error is how far the true mean could plausibly be from the sample mean at a chosen confidence level. It is the critical z value times the standard error. Solving for n tells you how big a sample you need for a desired margin.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to report the precision of a survey or experiment, or to plan the sample size.
assumptions: σ known (use t and s for small samples with unknown σ)

example.story: A sample of 100 has σ = 15. What is the 95 % margin of error for the mean?

formulas.name: Confidence interval for a mean (lower limit)

variables.name: lower limit
variables.description: Lower end of the confidence interval.

formulas.explanation: A confidence interval is a range built so that, over many repeated samples, the stated percentage of such ranges contain the true mean. Its lower limit is the sample mean minus the margin of error.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it with the upper limit to report an estimate of a population mean with its uncertainty.

example.story: A sample of 100 has mean 120 and σ = 15. Find the lower limit of the 95 % confidence interval.

formulas.name: Confidence interval for a mean (upper limit)

variables.name: upper limit
variables.description: Upper end of the confidence interval.

formulas.explanation: The upper limit is the sample mean plus the margin of error. Together with the lower limit it gives the interval x̄ ± z σ/√n. A wider interval gives more confidence but less precision.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it with the lower limit to report an interval estimate of a population mean.

example.story: A sample of 100 has mean 120 and σ = 15. Find the upper limit of the 95 % confidence interval.

formulas.name: Combinations (n choose r)

variables.name: number of combinations
variables.description: Ways to choose r items from n when order does not matter.

variables.name: number of items
variables.description: How many items there are to choose from.

variables.name: number chosen
variables.description: How many are picked (0 ≤ r ≤ n).

formulas.explanation: There are n!/(n - r)! ordered ways to pick r items, but every group of r items appears r! times in that list in different orders. Dividing by r! counts each group once. These numbers form Pascal's triangle and are the coefficients in the binomial theorem.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it when order does not matter: lottery tickets, committees, hands of cards, choosing which trials succeed.

example.story: In how many ways can a team of 3 be chosen from 10 students?

formulas.name: Permutations (arrangements)

variables.name: number of permutations
variables.description: Ordered ways to pick r items from n.

variables.name: number arranged
variables.description: How many positions are filled (0 ≤ r ≤ n).

formulas.explanation: For the first position there are n choices, then n - 1, and so on for r positions: n × (n - 1) × ... × (n - r + 1). That product equals n!/(n - r)!. Unlike combinations, ABC and CBA count as different.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it when order matters: podium places, codes without repeated digits, seating arrangements.

example.story: 8 runners race. In how many ways can gold, silver and bronze be awarded?

formulas.name: Binomial probability

variables.name: number of successes
variables.description: Exactly how many successes (0 ≤ k ≤ n).

variables.name: success probability
variables.description: Probability of success in one trial.

formulas.explanation: Any particular sequence with k successes and n - k failures has probability p^k (1 - p)^(n - k). The number of such sequences is n choose k, so multiply. The trials must be independent with the same p each time.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for a fixed number of independent yes/no trials: coin flips, defective items in a batch, correct guesses on a test.
assumptions: same probability of success each time

example.story: A fair coin is flipped 10 times. What is the probability of exactly 6 heads?

formulas.name: Mean of a binomial distribution

variables.name: expected number of successes
variables.description: The long-run average number of successes.

variables.name: success probability
variables.description: Probability of success in one trial.

formulas.explanation: Each trial contributes p successes on average, so n trials give np. For example, rolling a die 60 times you expect about 10 sixes, although the actual number varies.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find the expected number of successes in repeated independent trials.
assumptions: binomial setting: fixed n, independent trials, constant p

example.story: A die is rolled 20 times. How many sixes do you expect?

formulas.name: Variance of a binomial distribution

variables.name: standard deviation
variables.description: σ is the standard deviation of the number of successes; σ² is the variance.

variables.name: success probability
variables.description: Probability of success in one trial.

formulas.explanation: One trial has variance p(1 - p), which is largest when p = 0.5 and zero when the outcome is certain. Variances of independent trials add, giving np(1 - p) for n trials.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to describe how much the number of successes varies, or for a normal approximation to the binomial.
assumptions: binomial setting: fixed n, independent trials, constant p

example.story: A fair coin is flipped 20 times. Find the variance and standard deviation of the number of heads.

formulas.name: Poisson probability

variables.name: mean rate
variables.description: Average number of events in the interval.

formulas.explanation: The Poisson distribution counts random events that happen independently at a constant average rate, such as calls to a help desk per hour. Its mean and variance are both λ. It is also the limit of the binomial distribution for many trials with a small success probability.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for counts of rare or random events in a fixed time, area or volume: radioactive decays, typos per page, customers per minute.
assumptions: two events cannot happen at exactly the same moment

example.story: A help desk gets on average 3 calls per hour. What is the probability of exactly 5 calls in an hour?

formulas.name: Geometric distribution (first success)

variables.name: probability
variables.description: Probability that the first success happens on trial k.

variables.name: success probability
variables.description: Probability of success in each trial.

variables.name: trial number
variables.description: The trial on which the first success occurs (1, 2, 3, ...).

formulas.explanation: For the first success to come on trial k, the first k - 1 trials must all fail and trial k must succeed. Multiplying these independent probabilities gives the formula. The expected waiting time is 1/p trials.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for waiting-time questions: how many rolls until the first six, how many attempts until the first success.

example.story: What is the probability that the first six appears on the third roll of a die?

formulas.name: Expected value (two outcomes)
formulas.displayLatex: E(X) = \sum x_i p_i = p x_1 + (1 - p) x_2

variables.name: probability of the first outcome
variables.description: Probability of outcome x₁; the other outcome has 1 - p.

formulas.explanation: The expected value weights every outcome by its probability and adds them up. It is what you would average per play if you repeated the game many times. For more outcomes, add one term x p for each.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to judge whether a bet, game or decision pays off on average, or as the mean of a random variable.
assumptions: the probabilities of all outcomes add up to 1

example.story: A raffle ticket costs 1. With probability 0.01 you win 50 (a net gain of 49), otherwise you lose your 1. What is the expected gain?
steps: E = 0.49 - 0.99 = -0.5, a loss of 0.5 per ticket on average

formulas.name: Probability of equally likely outcomes

variables.name: probability of A
variables.description: The chance that event A happens.

variables.name: favourable outcomes
variables.description: Number of outcomes in event A.

variables.name: possible outcomes
variables.description: Total number of equally likely outcomes.

formulas.explanation: When every outcome is equally likely, the probability of an event is the fraction of outcomes that belong to it. A probability of 0 means impossible and 1 means certain.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for fair dice, coins, well-shuffled cards and random draws.

example.story: A card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability that it is a heart?

formulas.name: Complement rule

variables.name: probability of not A
variables.description: The chance that A does not happen.

formulas.explanation: Either A happens or it does not, so the two probabilities add up to 1. Working out the complement is often easier, as in the probability of at least one six in several rolls, which is 1 minus the probability of no sixes.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for 'at least one' problems and whenever the opposite event is easier to count.

example.story: The chance of rain tomorrow is 0.3. What is the chance it stays dry?

formulas.name: Addition rule (A or B)
formulas.displayLatex: P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)

variables.name: probability of A or B
variables.description: Chance that at least one of A and B happens.

formulas.explanation: Adding P(A) and P(B) counts the outcomes in both events twice, so the overlap is subtracted once. For mutually exclusive events the overlap is zero and the probabilities simply add.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for 'either or both' questions, such as drawing a heart or a king.

example.story: A card is drawn from a 52-card deck. What is the probability of a heart or a king?

formulas.name: Multiplication rule for independent events
formulas.explanation: Two events are independent when one happening does not change the chance of the other. Then the probability that both happen is the product of their probabilities. This equation is also the test for independence.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for separate coin flips, dice rolls, or draws with replacement.
assumptions: A and B are independent (otherwise use P(A) P(B | A))

example.story: Two dice are rolled. What is the probability that both show a six?

formulas.name: Conditional probability

variables.name: probability of A given B
variables.description: Chance of A when you already know B happened.

formulas.explanation: Knowing that B happened shrinks the set of possibilities to B. The chance of A is then the part of B where A also happens, as a fraction of all of B. In a two-way table it is a cell divided by its row or column total.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it whenever information changes the odds: medical tests, two-way tables, drawing without replacement.

example.story: In a school, 40 % of students play sport and 12 % play sport and music. What fraction of the sporty students play music?

formulas.name: Bayes' theorem

variables.name: posterior
variables.description: Probability of A after observing B.

variables.name: likelihood
variables.description: Probability of observing B if A is true.

variables.name: prior
variables.description: Probability of A before the observation.

formulas.explanation: Bayes' theorem turns P(B | A) around into P(A | B). Both equal P(A and B) divided by something, which links them. It explains why a positive result for a rare disease is often a false alarm: the prior P(A) is small.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to update a probability with new evidence: diagnostic tests, spam filters, forensic evidence.
assumptions: P(B) usually comes from the law of total probability

example.story: A disease affects 1 % of people. A test detects it 95 % of the time, and 5.9 % of all tests come back positive. If you test positive, what is the chance you have the disease?

formulas.name: Law of total probability

variables.name: B given A
variables.description: Chance of B when A is true.

variables.name: B given not A
variables.description: Chance of B when A is false.

formulas.explanation: B can happen in two separate ways: with A or without A. Add the probabilities of both branches of the tree diagram. This gives the denominator needed in Bayes' theorem.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it with tree diagrams to find an overall probability from conditional ones.
assumptions: A and not A cover all cases

example.story: 1 % of people have a disease. The test is positive for 95 % of those with it and 5 % of those without it. What fraction of all tests are positive?

formulas.name: Pearson correlation coefficient

variables.name: correlation coefficient
variables.description: Strength and direction of the linear relationship, from -1 to 1.

formulas.explanation: r measures how closely points lie along a straight line. S_xy is positive when x and y tend to be above or below their means together, and dividing by √(S_xx S_yy) scales the result to lie between -1 and 1. Values near ±1 mean a strong linear relationship; correlation does not prove causation.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to describe the strength of a linear relationship in paired data, for example height and arm span.

example.story: Paired data give S_xy = 42, S_xx = 50 and S_yy = 40. Find the correlation coefficient.

formulas.name: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient

variables.name: rank correlation
variables.description: Agreement between two rankings, from -1 to 1.

variables.name: sum of squared rank differences
variables.description: Σd², where d is the difference between the two ranks of each item.

formulas.explanation: Rank each variable separately, then compare the ranks. If the rankings agree perfectly every d is 0 and r_s = 1; if they are exactly reversed r_s = -1. Because it uses ranks, it detects any monotonic relationship and is not upset by outliers.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for ranked data, such as two judges scoring contestants, or when the relationship is not linear.
assumptions: this simple formula assumes no tied ranks

example.story: Two judges rank 8 dancers. The squared differences between their ranks add up to 10. How well do they agree?

formulas.name: Least squares regression slope

variables.name: slope
variables.description: Gradient of the best-fit line y = a + b x.

formulas.explanation: The least squares line makes the total of the squared vertical distances from the points to the line as small as possible. Calculus shows its gradient is S_xy / S_xx, and the line always passes through the mean point (x̄, ȳ).
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to fit a straight line to paired data for prediction, such as fuel use against distance.
assumptions: predict y from x (not the other way round)

example.story: Paired data give S_xy = 42 and S_xx = 50. Find the gradient of the regression line of y on x.

formulas.name: Least squares regression intercept

variables.name: intercept
variables.description: Value of y on the regression line when x = 0.

formulas.explanation: The least squares line passes through the mean point (x̄, ȳ). Substituting that point into y = a + b x and rearranging gives the intercept.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it after finding the slope to complete the regression equation y = a + b x.
assumptions: the intercept may have no real meaning if x = 0 is far outside the data

example.story: Data have x̄ = 10 and ȳ = 20, and the regression slope is 0.84. Find the intercept.
steps: a = 11.6, so the line is y = 11.6 + 0.84x
